problemText: What does register mean in writing? Choose the definition that matches what you learned in class.
choices: The specific pitch and volume a speaker produces when delivering words out loud to an audience
The official record or log that documents the names and contact details of attendees at a particular gathering or event
How formal or informal a piece of writing needs to be for its audience and purpose
The method by which a writer structures and arranges the sequence of paragraphs to guide readers from start to finish
hints: Think about the difference between writing a school report and texting a friend.
Register is about the level of formality you choose at the start and keep throughout.

problemText: Read this sentence from a thank-you letter to your grandmother: 'The gift was absolutely fire, no cap.' The rest of the letter uses warm, everyday words like 'so happy' and 'loved spending time with you.' Why is this sentence a problem in the letter?
choices: It is a sentence fragment and needs to be fixed with standard grammar
It does not tell the reader what gift you received from your grandmother
It is too short compared to the other sentences in the letter
It uses slang and casual filler words that do not match the warm but respectful register of the rest of the letter
hints: The lesson says a lapse can be a perfectly correct sentence — the problem is not grammar but register.
Look at what signals a casual register: slang, casual filler words, and exaggeration.

problemText: A student is writing a formal announcement about a field trip for the school website. Most sentences use careful, precise wording like 'Students will depart from the main entrance at 8:30 a.m.' and 'All participants must bring a packed lunch.' Which sentence would break the formal register of this announcement?
choices: Honestly, the aquarium is literally the coolest place ever, and you should totally go if you can.
Chaperones will monitor and assist students during the entire scheduled visit to the aquarium facility.
All permission slips must be completed, signed by a parent or guardian, and delivered by the deadline of Wednesday.
The transportation bus will arrive back at school by 3:00 p.m., ensuring students meet the afternoon dismissal schedule.
hints: Formal register uses precise vocabulary and no slang — look for casual filler words in the choices.
Which sentence uses words like 'honestly,' 'literally,' and 'totally' that do not fit a school announcement?

problemText: Read this short book review for a school assignment: 'The novel follows a young hero on a dangerous quest to save her village. The author builds tension throughout the story with sharp, suspenseful dialogue. We were literally so hyped while reading the last chapter because the ending was insane. The book teaches important lessons about courage and loyalty.' Identify the sentence that breaks the formal, informative tone and explain why it is the lapse.
choices: The first sentence is the lapse because it uses the word 'hero,' which is too casual for a formal review.
The third sentence is the lapse because it uses slang and casual filler words that do not match the careful, precise wording of the other sentences.
The second sentence is the lapse because it uses the word 'author,' which does not belong in a book review.
The fourth sentence is the lapse because it mentions lessons, which is not appropriate for a school assignment.
hints: First, read the other three sentences and decide what register most of the review is using.
Look for casual filler words and slang signals, then compare the sentence with the register that the rest of the piece established.

problemText: A student wrote this informal text to a friend about a weekend project: 'I finally finished painting my bedroom this weekend and it looks so awesome. We went to the store twice because we did not have enough paint for the first coat. Upon reflection, the acquisition of appropriate materials in advance would have facilitated the completion of said endeavor. I cannot wait to show you the finished room when you visit next month.' Which sentence is the lapse, and what should the student do to fix it?
choices: The first sentence is the lapse; rewrite it to use casual, everyday wording like the rest of the text.
The second sentence is the lapse; rewrite it to use slang and exaggeration to match the informal tone.
The third sentence is the lapse; rewrite it in casual, friendly wording that keeps the same information.
The fourth sentence is the lapse; rewrite it to match the formal vocabulary of the other sentences.
hints: Identify which register most of the text uses by reading the first, second, and fourth sentences together.
The lapse will have formal, stiff vocabulary that does not match the warm, casual wording the rest of the piece already established.

problemText: A student is revising a formal email to a museum director requesting a group visit. The student has identified this sentence as breaking the register: 'The field trip would be educational for our students and help them learn about art history, which would be sick.' Which of the following revisions best fixes the lapse by keeping the same information in the established formal register?
choices: The field trip would be educational for our students and help them learn about art history, and that sounds pretty good.
The field trip would help our sixth-grade students gain knowledge about art history because it is literally the best way to learn.
The field trip would teach our students about art history, and honestly, it would be really awesome for everyone.
The field trip would be an excellent educational opportunity that allows our students to deepen their understanding of art history.
hints: A proper fix replaces the slang word 'sick' with formal, precise vocabulary while preserving the core information about the field trip's educational value.
Check each choice: Does it remove the casual register completely and use careful word choice that matches a formal email to an official?

problemText: A nonrestrictive element is information that a sentence does not need in order to identify what it is talking about. Which sentence contains a nonrestrictive element that is correctly set off with commas?
choices: My best friend Sophia won the spelling bee yesterday.
My best friend, Sophia, won the spelling bee yesterday.
My best friend, Sophia won the spelling bee yesterday.
The student who studied hardest won the spelling bee yesterday.
hints: Use the removal test: cover the name Sophia and see if you can still tell who you are talking about.
When the extra information sits in the middle of a sentence, it needs a matching pair of marks on both sides.

problemText: Jordan has three sisters. One of them is named Maya. Which sentence is punctuated correctly for this situation?
choices: Jordan's sister, Maya, always helps him with homework.
Jordan's sister — Maya — always helps him with homework.
Jordan's sister Maya always helps him with homework.
Jordan's sister, Maya always helps him with homework.
hints: Run the removal test: if Jordan has three sisters, does the name Maya help identify which one?
Restrictive information — information the sentence needs — takes no commas at all.

problemText: The soccer team has only one goalie, and her name is Iris. A student writes: 'Our goalie Iris is the fastest runner on the team.' This sentence is missing punctuation. Which version corrects the mistake?
choices: Our goalie, Iris is the fastest runner on the team.
Our goalie Iris, is the fastest runner on the team.
Our goalie — Iris is the fastest runner on the team.
Our goalie, Iris, is the fastest runner on the team.
hints: The name Iris sits in the middle of the sentence and needs marks on both sides.
A matching pair means you open with one mark and close with the exact same kind of mark.

problemText: There is only one principal at the school, and the student wants to set off extra information with a pair of dashes instead of commas. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
choices: Our principal — Dr. Nakamura — announced a surprise assembly during the morning announcements.
Our principal, Dr. Nakamura — announced a surprise assembly during the morning announcements.
Our principal — Dr. Nakamura, announced a surprise assembly during the morning announcements.
Our principal Dr. Nakamura — announced a surprise assembly during the morning announcements.
hints: Dashes do the same job as commas: they set off nonrestrictive information.
When you use dashes, you must use matching marks — one before the extra information and one after it.

problemText: A student has written two sentences and needs to decide which one is punctuated correctly. The class has only one art teacher. Which sentence correctly reports this fact?
choices: The art teacher who teaches painting and sculpture is Mr. Chen.
The art teacher, who teaches painting and sculpture, is Mr. Chen.
The art teacher, who teaches painting and sculpture is Mr. Chen.
The art teacher who teaches painting and sculpture, is Mr. Chen.
hints: Use the removal test on the clause 'who teaches painting and sculpture.' If there is only one art teacher, can you still tell who is meant without this clause?
When a nonrestrictive clause sits in the middle of a sentence, it needs matching marks — one before and one after — to set it off completely.

problemText: A writer has two different facts to share and wants to punctuate the same sentence two different ways. Fact 1: The restaurant has only one chef. Fact 2: The restaurant has multiple chefs. How should the sentence be punctuated differently for each fact?
choices: For both facts, the sentence should be 'The restaurant's chef Marco creates daily specials' with no commas because the name always identifies which chef.
For both facts, the sentence should be 'The restaurant's chef, Marco, creates daily specials' because a person's name is always set off with commas.
For Fact 1: 'The restaurant's chef, Marco, creates daily specials' (name is extra). For Fact 2: 'The restaurant's chef Marco creates daily specials' (name identifies which chef).
For Fact 1: 'The restaurant's chef Marco creates daily specials' (name is restrictive). For Fact 2: 'The restaurant's chef, Marco, creates daily specials' (name is extra).
hints: The removal test tells you whether information is restrictive or nonrestrictive, and that depends on the fact about how many chefs there are.
The same words in the same order can be punctuated differently depending on what the sentence needs to identify.

problemText: A complete sentence needs three things. Which group of words has all three—a subject, a verb, and a finished thought?
choices: The rain falling hard on the roof while we watched.
Because the rain fell hard on the roof.
Fell hard on the roof during the storm.
The rain fell hard on the roof.
hints: Ask yourself: Who or what is it about? What do they do or are? Does it leave you waiting for more information?
A starter word like because makes the thought unfinished, even if there is a subject and verb.

problemText: Read this group of words: "When the game ended in overtime." Use the three-part test to find what is wrong with it.
choices: It has a subject and verb but is a fragment because a starter word holds it open.
It is missing a verb, which means it cannot form a complete independent clause on its own.
It is a run-on sentence because it incorrectly joins two separate complete thoughts without proper punctuation.
It is missing a subject, so there is no noun to tell who or what the sentence is about.
hints: The word 'when' is a starter word—does it leave you waiting to hear what happened?
Check if there is a subject (the game) and a verb (ended). The problem is not missing those.

problemText: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: After the store closed early we had to go shopping the next day.
After the store closed early, we had to go shopping the next day.
After the store closed early we had to go shopping, the next day.
After the store closed early the store closed, we had to go shopping.
hints: A starter word group at the beginning of a sentence needs to be set off by a comma.
Look for a group of words that begins with a starter word and check if the comma comes in the right place.

problemText: Read this sentence: "The soccer team practiced in the rain, they did not want to miss the scrimmage." Identify the error and choose the best way to fix it.
choices: Move the second clause first: They did not want to miss the scrimmage, the soccer team practiced in the rain.
Use a joining word with a comma: The soccer team practiced in the rain, because they did not want to miss the scrimmage.
Use a period: The soccer team practiced in the rain. They did not want to miss the scrimmage.
Delete the comma: The soccer team practiced in the rain they did not want to miss the scrimmage.
hints: Two complete sentences joined by only a comma is called a comma splice. Check which fix is legal.
Fixes for a comma splice include a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a joining word—but the joining word should show how the ideas connect.

problemText: A student wrote: "Although the recipe called for three eggs we used two instead." Which revision correctly fixes this error without changing the meaning too much?
choices: Although the recipe called for three eggs, we used two instead.
We used two eggs although the recipe called for three eggs.
Although the recipe called for three eggs, we used two instead, which was fine.
Both A and B are correct.
hints: A starter word can come at the beginning or the end. Think about where the comma goes in each case.
Review the rule: starter word at the front gets a comma after it; starter word at the end needs no comma between the two parts.

problemText: A student wrote three versions of the same idea. Read all three and decide which one has NO error at all. "(1) Because I left my homework at school. I had to redo it at home. (2) I left my homework at school I had to redo it at home. (3) Since I left my homework at school, I had to redo it at home."
choices: Version 3 is correct because a starter word is properly attached to a complete sentence with a comma.
Version 2 is correct because it joins two complete thoughts without any extra punctuation marks between them.
Version 1 is correct because it separates the starter-word group from the complete sentence with a period, making two statements.
Version 2 is correct because the two complete sentences are placed side by side to show they are related to each other.
hints: Version 1 has a period between a starter-word group and a complete sentence. Is that legal?
Version 2 joins two complete sentences with no punctuation. Version 3 joins a starter-word group to a complete sentence with proper punctuation. Which one obeys the rules?

problemText: Read this paragraph from a sports blog: 'Maya hit the ball. Maya ran to first base. Maya slid into second base.' What repeated pattern makes this paragraph sound choppy?
choices: The word 'base' appears twice in a row.
Every sentence starts with the exact same word, Maya.
All three sentences are exactly the same length.
The sentences use too many action verbs.
hints: Look at the first word of each sentence in the paragraph.
The lesson says the repeated pattern a reader notices first is what comes at the start of the sentences.

problemText: Here are two correct sentences from a recipe: 'The timer went off. Everyone grabbed a plate.' What is left unstated between these two sentences?
choices: Whether the timer was mechanical, digital, or electronic and which brand was purchased.
The specific emotions or motivations that caused each person individually to want to grab a plate at that moment.
The reason or timing that connects one event to the other.
The exact number of minutes the timer had been set for before it began to ring.
hints: Two separate sentences side by side make the reader guess how they connect.
A connector word like 'when' or 'so' would state this relationship.

problemText: A student wrote this paragraph for the school newspaper: 'The lights went out. The crowd gasped. The spotlight came on. Everyone cheered.' The student wants to fix the choppy rhythm without changing any facts or adding words that do not belong. Which revision fixes this problem?
choices: The lights went out and the crowd gasped loudly. The spotlight came on and everyone cheered with excitement.
The lights went out because the crowd gasped. The spotlight came on so everyone cheered.
The lights suddenly went out. The crowd gasped dramatically. The spotlight came on brightly. Everyone cheered wildly.
When the lights went out, the crowd gasped. After the spotlight came on, everyone cheered.
hints: The original has 'The' opening four sentences in a row — that is the choppy pattern.
A real fix either removes a repeated opener or adds a connector that states a relationship.

problemText: A student is revising these two sentences for the class website: 'The storm rolled in quickly. The soccer game was cancelled.' The student adds a connector to show how these events relate: 'Because the storm rolled in quickly, the soccer game was cancelled.' Is this a real fix according to the rules of sentence variety, and why?
choices: Yes, because the connector 'because' states the relationship between the two events without changing what happened.
No, because combining sentences always removes important detail and loses the impact of having two separate statements.
No, because the word 'because' is too casual for a website and should be replaced with a more formal connector instead.
Yes, because it removes a repeated opening word that appeared three times in a row.
hints: A real fix does one of two things: it removes a repeated opener, or it adds a connector that states a relationship.
Check whether the facts of what happened changed — they should not.

problemText: A student wrote this paragraph for a class essay: 'I organized my notes. I sorted them by topic. I made flashcards. I studied for thirty minutes. I felt ready for the test.' The student wants to fix the choppy rhythm. The student tries two different revisions. Revision A: 'I organized my notes, sorted them by topic, and made flashcards. I studied for thirty minutes and felt ready for the test.' Revision B: 'After organizing my notes and sorting them by topic, I made flashcards. Then I studied for thirty minutes. Finally, I felt ready for the test.' Both revisions keep all the original facts. Which revision is the better fix, and what is the main reason?
choices: Revision B is better because it adds more connectors like 'after' and 'then' that state relationships.
Revision A is better because it removes more repeated 'I' openers at the start of sentences.
They are equally good fixes because both change the rhythm without adding or removing any facts.
Revision A is better because it makes the sentences longer, which always improves sentence variety.
hints: Count how many times 'I' opens a sentence in each revision.
The lesson says that removing a word repeated three or more times in a row is a testable reason a revision counts as a real fix.
